title: Nature/Nurture
cheat_card: Most animal behaviors have a genetic basis (nature) but are modulated by environmental influences (nurture), linked to the nervous and endocrine systems.

Nest-building in lovebirds demonstrates genetic control: Fischer's lovebirds carry material in their beaks, peach-faced lovebirds tuck strips in feathers, and their hybrids show intermediate, confused behaviors.
Garter snake food choice is genetically wired: inland populations eat fish/frogs and refuse slugs, coastal populations eat slugs, and their hybrids accept slugs.
Human twin studies (e.g., Scott & Mark Kelly) show twins separated at birth share similar food preferences, activity levels, and mate selection.
Maternal nurturing behavior in mice post-birth depends on the expression of a single gene called fosB; mutating it leads to pup neglect.
memory_anchor: Genetics of Behavior: Lovebirds (beak vs feather nesting hybrids), Garter Snakes (inland refuse vs coastal accept slug hybrids), Mice (fosB gene deletion causes maternal neglect).

flashcards.q: What experimental evidence from lovebird hybrid breeding supports the idea that behavior has a genetic basis?
flashcards.a: Fischer lovebirds carry nesting material in their beaks, while peach-faced lovebirds tuck it into their feathers. Hybrid offspring attempt both methods and exhibit extreme difficulty carrying materials, proving nest-building behavior is genetically inherited.

flashcards.q: How does the diet of coastal and inland garter snakes, along with their hybrids, demonstrate the genetic basis of behavior?
flashcards.a: Inland snakes feed on frogs and fish and refuse slugs, while coastal snakes feed on slugs. Hybrid offspring accept slugs as a food source, indicating that slug preference is a genetically controlled trait.

flashcards.q: What genetic factor determines post-birth maternal nurturing behavior in mice, and what happens when it is mutated?
flashcards.a: Maternal nurturing behavior is dependent on the presence of a single gene termed fosB. When both copies of the fosB gene are inactive, the mother mouse neglects her pups, failing to retrieve or warm them.

outline_blanks: Experiments with lovebirds, garter snakes, and mice show that behavior has a genetic basis. For example, nest-building hybrids of Fischer and peach-faced lovebirds show confusion, and maternal care in mice depends on a single gene named [[fosB]]. Similarly, coastal garter snakes accept [[slugs]] as food, whereas inland snakes refuse them, with hybrids showing intermediate acceptance.
